Fixing a Knowledge Graph Problem Nobody Talks About…
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Three posts ago I argued that similarity is not comprehension. Two posts ago, that a knowledge graph framework should be pluggable across domains rather than rebuilt for each one. Last post, that a flat graph loses the kind of claim each edge represents, and that recovering it needs a second, epistemic layer.
All three were about making the graph better. None addressed the question that actually decides whether a knowledge graph gets used: what happens the day after you build it?
The honest failure mode goes like this. You run the pipeline. You get a beautiful graph. You answer your question.
Then a colleague asks for it and you cannot share much beyond the results.
Then three new papers publish and you rebuild from scratch.
Then someone asks “when did we start believing that?” — and there’s no answer, because the graph only ever knew its present tense.
A graph that lives for one session is a query result. A graph that survives, accumulates, and can be handed to someone else is an asset.
Three things shipped over the last two months to close that gap. They map onto the three questions anyone asks about a new tool, in order: Can I keep it? Can I trust it? Can I share it?

Press enter or click to view image in full size

1. Keep it — projects that grow
Epistract used to think in runs: point it at a folder, get an output directory. Fine once. Useless for a research program.
It now thinks in projects — named, reusable knowledge bases, each with its own corpus, graph, epistemic layer and search index.
epistract init glp1-landscape --domain drug-discovery
epistract add files ./papers/*.pdf --project glp1-landscape
epistract index --project glp1-landscape
epistract search "GLP-1 receptor agonist" --project glp1-landscape --expandDocuments deduplicate by content, not filename — the same paper downloaded twice is one document. Indexing is incremental, so adding five papers to a corpus of two hundred costs five papers’ worth of work. And --expand walks the graph: search is hybrid, a zero-server full-text index over entities and chunks, fused by reciprocal rank, with optional PageRank expansion across relations.
Deleting a project never touches your source documents. That sounds minor until you’ve done it by accident somewhere else.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

2. Trust it — the graph checks its own work
This started as a literature review rather than a feature. I ran a structured sweep of 35 papers on graph construction, entity resolution, hallucination detection and temporal reasoning. Eleven were adopted. Seven deferred. Seventeen rejected — including some famous ones. The rejections matter as much as the adoptions: this is a framework with a thesis, and techniques that contradict it don’t get in because they’re popular.
The eleven survivors became one command — epistract enhance — in three passes:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

That last pass changes what the graph is. Most systems overwrite. Epistract invalidates and keeps the record, stamped with when it changed and what superseded it. The graph stops being a snapshot of current belief and becomes a record of how belief moved.
Everything runs offline with lexical fallbacks; --llm swaps in a model where one genuinely helps.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

3. Share it — OKF, and why this is the one to care about
If I could only ship one of the three, it would be this.
Epistract now exports to OKF (Open Knowledge Format) — Google’s formalization of the “LLM-wiki” pattern: knowledge published as a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter, where file paths are concept IDs and links form the graph. Git-versionable. Tool-agnostic. Readable by humans and AI agents alike.
epistract export --format okf --project glp1-landscape --out ./glp1-kbWhat comes out isn’t an export artifact. It’s a knowledge base you can commit on git!:
glp1-kb/
├── index.md # root index
├── log.md # dated record of superseded claims
├── compounds/
│ ├── semaglutide.md
│ └── tirzepatide.md
├── claims/
└── graph_data.json # lossless native sidecarOpen any concept file in any markdown viewer:
---
epistract_id: semaglutide
epistract_confidence: 0.97
tags: [contested, glp1-agonists]
---# Relations| Relation | Target | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|------------------------|-----------:|-----------|
| INDICATED_FOR | obesity | 0.97 | asserted |
| INDICATED_FOR | cardiovascular disease | 0.62 | prophetic |The epistemic layer survives the trip. Status is a column. Contested and superseded edges become tags. Superseded claims become dated entries in log.md. And by spec, OKF consumers preserve unknown frontmatter keys — so the epistract_* fields reach downstream tooling intact.
The example that makes it click
Month 1. You build glp1-landscape from 24 papers and 10 patents. Export OKF. git init. Commit.
Month 3. Head-to-head trial data publishes. Three commands — add files, index, enhance. The bi-temporal pass finds the new result contradicts an older efficacy claim, marks the old edge superseded, and points it at the winner. Export again, commit, then:
git diff HEAD~1 -- compounds/semaglutide.md- | INDICATED_FOR | obesity | 0.62 | prophetic |
+ | INDICATED_FOR | obesity | 0.97 | asserted |Your knowledge graph now has a commit history. That one property unlocks things that used to be projects unto themselves:

• Review knowledge like code. A change in what your organization believes arrives as a pull request. Your domain expert comments on the exact line where a claim moved from prophetic to asserted. Approval is a merge.

• Answer “when did we know this?” — git log on a concept file, plus log.md for what it replaced.

• Hand it to anyone. They read markdown. No graph database, no query language, no Epistract install, no onboarding call.

• Feed any AI agent. Point Claude, an internal copilot, or a RAG pipeline at the folder — that’s what the format was built for. Unlike a vector index, what the agent reads carries typed relations, confidence, provenance and epistemic status.

• No lock-in, credibly. Markdown for humans and agents, plus a lossless JSON sidecar for exact round-trip.
One operational note for regulated or confidential work: --no-evidence strips verbatim source quotes from the bundle, the sidecar and the claims layer. The docs treat that as required, not optional, whenever a bundle leaves your machine and the corpus isn't already public.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

So who is this actually for?
Scientists and analysts: you have a corpus and a bounded question. Epistract turns it into a structured, cited graph in an afternoon, tells you which claims are demonstrated versus merely staked, keeps the graph as you add sources, and gives you a folder you can attach to a review. Proven across eight validated corpora in five domains — biomedical literature and patents, trial protocols, regulatory labels, adverse-event reports, contracts — at 7–34 documents each, deliberately the size a specialist actually curates.
IT and data leaders: a knowledge-graph capability that needs no new infrastructure. No graph database to provision, no ontology committee. The persistence layer is git, which you already run. A new domain is four config files and about fifteen minutes, not a quarter of platform work. MIT-licensed, so evaluation doesn’t route through legal. And the output feeds your existing AI stack without an integration project.
What I haven’t seen combined anywhere else: per-edge epistemic typing, bi-temporal invalidation that preserves superseded claims, and a portable format carrying both into plain files your version control can diff. Any one exists somewhere. Together they produce a knowledge asset that records not just what you know, but what you used to think and when that changed.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

What’s still missing

• OKF claims/ export is contracts-shaped only. Domains on the older claims schema — drug-discovery included — currently produce zero files under claims/, with no warning. Graph and relations export fine. First on the list.

• OKF import is deferred, deliberately. Markdown-to-graph import would yield untyped edges with no confidence or evidence — exactly the signal the epistemic layer depends on — plus a prompt-injection surface in third-party bundles.

• Still no cross-run learning. Lessons from one project don’t fold into the next. Tracked publicly as Issue #15, still open.

Try it, and tell me what breaks
/plugin marketplace add usathyan/epistract
/plugin install epistract
/epistract:setupPoint it at a corpus you actually care about — the messier and further from life sciences, the more useful your feedback. Still MIT, still built on evenings and weekends, all eight scenarios and their artifacts committed to the repo.
Repo: github.com/usathyan/epistract · OKF mapping: docs/OKF-MAPPING.md · Projects: docs/PROJECTS.md
Two questions I’d genuinely like answers to:

• Is OKF/git the right persistence layer for organizational knowledge? It feels obviously correct to me, and I’m suspicious of that.

• Has anyone built review workflows over a knowledge graph? Pull-requests-for-knowledge seems powerful and under-explored. If you’ve tried it, I want to hear how it went.
